q-73565:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot 6-4\cdot 3 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is false, all the other parts of the theorem are false too. Therefore, according to the theorem: 

- Statement II is false by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is true by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

q-47652:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ -5 & k\end{aligned}] \\  & =5\cdot k-(-1)\cdot (-5) \\  & =5k-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $5k-5\ne 0$ if $k\ne 1.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be a unique zero solution to $Ax=0.$

- Statement III is true. According to the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.

Finally, only statements I and III are true.

q-73608:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

Let $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{aligned}].$ If $k\ne 1$, then

$$
det(A)=det[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{aligned}]=1-k\ne 0.
$$

So, according to the invertible matrix theorem $A$ is invertible and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is the unique solution of  $Ax=0.$
Also, the system 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
has exactly one solution, and the lines $x+y=0$ and $x+ky=0$ intersect at exactly one point. 

Therefore, the true statement is as follows:

*If $k\ne 1$, then the system $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the unique zero solution.* $\,✓$

q-128144:
First, notice that

$$
(f(t)-2g(t))^{′}={f}^{′}(t)-2{g}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t-1})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,\frac{1}{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩ \\ {g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f(1)-2g(1))^{′} & ={f}^{′}(1)-2{g}^{′}(1) \\  & =⟨2(1),\,\frac{1}{1},\,{e}^{1-1}⟩-2⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}},\,3(1)^{2},\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,1,1⟩-2⟨1,3,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,1,1⟩-⟨2,6,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-5,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-127998:
By the sum rule, we have

$$
(f(t)+g(t))^{′}={f}^{′}(t)+{g}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's find the derivatives of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t-1)^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,2t,\,2(t-1)⟩ \\ {g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f(t)+g(t))^{′} & ={f}^{′}(t)+{g}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-2,\,2t,\,2t-2⟩+⟨1,\,-2,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,2t-2,\,3{t}^{2}+2t-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-71233:
Using the scalar function multiple rule, we can write

$$
{(u(t)f(t))}^{′}={u}^{′}(t)f(t)+u(t){f}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's find ${u}^{′}(t)$ and ${f}^{′}(t).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-7)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2} \\ 2t \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u(t)f(t))}^{′} & ={u}^{′}(t)f(t)+u(t){f}^{′}(t) \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{3}-3 \\ {t}^{2}+1 \\ 4t-7\end{aligned}]+{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2} \\ 2t \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(2{t}^{3}-3){e}^{t} \\ ({t}^{2}+1){e}^{t} \\ (4t-7){e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2}{e}^{t} \\ 2t{e}^{t} \\ 4{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{2}-3){e}^{t} \\ ({t}^{2}+2t+1){e}^{t} \\ (4t-3){e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-70688:
Using the scalar function multiple rule, we can write

$$
(u(t)f(t))^{′}={u}^{′}(t)f(t)+u(t){f}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's find ${u}^{′}(t)$ and ${f}^{′}(t).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(u(t)f(t))^{′} & ={u}^{′}(t)f(t)+u(t){f}^{′}(t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+\operatorname{sin}⁡t[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {cos}^{2}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ -{sin}^{2}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-70695:
Using the chain rule, we can write

$$
(f∘u)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(u) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{cos}⁡u) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\,({u}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}⁡u)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 3{u}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘u)^{′}(t) & ={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u(t)) \\ 3(u(t))^{2} \\ \frac{1}{u(t)}\end{aligned}]\cdot {u}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t}) \\ 3({e}^{t})^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\end{aligned}]\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t}) \\ 3{e}^{2t} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\end{aligned}]\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t}){e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{3t} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-128561:
Using the chain rule, we can write

$$
(f∘u)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}⁡u)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({u}^{2})j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\sqrt{u})k \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\,i+2u\,j+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\,k \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})=-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘u)^{′}(t) & ={f}^{′}(u(t))\cdot {u}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{u(t)}\,i+2u(t)\,j+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u(t)}}\,k)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{e}^{-t}}}\,k)\cdot (-{e}^{-t}) \\  & =({e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t/2}\,k)\cdot (-{e}^{-t}) \\  & =-\,i-2{e}^{-2t}\,j-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t/2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

q-32347:
Using the cross product rule, we can write:

$$
(f\times g)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times {g}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6)⟩ \\  & =⟨12t,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ {g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,6t,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t)\times g(t) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 12t & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 3{t}^{2} & (4t-1)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 3{t}^{2} & (4t-1)\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}12t & 0 \\ 3 & (4t-1)\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}12t & 2 \\ 3 & 3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =⟨8t-2,\,12t-48{t}^{2},\,36{t}^{3}-6⟩ \\ f(t)\times {g}^{′}(t) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 6{t}^{2} & 2t & 6 \\ 0 & 6t & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2t & 6 \\ 6t & 4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2} & 6 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2} & 2t \\ 0 & 6t\end{aligned}|k \\  & =⟨-28t,\,-24{t}^{2},\,36{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\times g)^{′}(t) & =⟨8t-2,\,12t-48{t}^{2},\,36{t}^{3}-6⟩+⟨-28t,\,-24{t}^{2},\,36{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨-20t-2,\,-72{t}^{2}+12t,\,72{t}^{3}-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Using the cross product rule, we can write:

$$
(f\times g)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times {g}^{′}(t)

q-142562:
If the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have joint distribution with joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & ={f}_{X}(x)={\sum }_{y}f(x,y) \\ P(Y=y) & ={f}_{Y}(y)={\sum }_{x}f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

In this case, the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Let's add these row and column totals to our table:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.25$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.4$ | $0.05$ | $0.45$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.1$ | $0.15$ | $0.25$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.55$ | $0.45$ | $1$ |
